items.title: Anthropic ships Claude Mods — plugins can now hook deeper into Claude Code's own behavior
items.summary: Claude Code 2.1.287 added Claude Mods: plugins are no longer limited to slash commands and subagents, they can now modify deeper behavior, the same way a browser extension reaches into a page. The same release ships a built-in example, "You should know" — a side agent that watches your session and flags things you or Claude might miss (enable with /plugin enable cc-plugin-you-should-know@builtin).
items.why: The plugin system just stopped being a way to add commands and became an actual extension API you can hook into live sessions with.
items.action: Run /plugin enable cc-plugin-you-should-know@builtin on your next session and see what it catches, then skim the mods/hooks docs if you want to write your own.

eval.reason: Claude Mods is a genuine new extension point (plugins can modify deeper session behavior), not a routine version bump.

items.title: OpenAI ships dots — always-on agents that investigate bugs and prep PRs while you're away
items.summary: Dots run continuously on their own cloud compute, connect to 4,000+ apps, and do proactive background work. OpenAI's own developer examples: a dot investigating a bug report and preparing a pull request with a test video attached, and building/testing improvements from customer feedback without step-by-step direction.
items.why: This is OpenAI's answer to "keep working after I close the laptop" — point a dot at an open bug and it can come back with a ready PR instead of waiting for you to start a session.
items.action: Watch the dots demo, then point one at a real open issue in a side project to see what it comes back with.

eval.reason: A genuinely new always-on agent product, not an incremental update to an existing one.

items.title: An engineer open-sourced a self-hosted, open-weights clone of a popular typed-decision API
items.summary: A self-hosted project (jev-vllm) reimplements a hosted typed-decision API, running an open-weights model on your own GPU via vLLM + KServe. Measured on one NVIDIA GB10: 79ms p50 (~13 decisions/s), up to 94 decisions/s at 32 concurrent requests, no per-call cost, nothing leaves your hardware. Ships with a full working example: a fully local voice-controlled browser that acts mid-sentence.
items.why: This turns "ask an LLM for yes/no instead of a paragraph" from a hosted-only pattern into something you can run and tune yourself, with real measured numbers instead of a vendor's claims.
items.action: The repo's client/payloads/ has a working request for every question type — clone it and point one at a real decision point in a side project (route this ticket, is this change risky) and compare latency/cost against just calling an LLM for the same judgment.

eval.reason: A real open-source release with measured performance numbers, not a reshare of old news.

items.title: A healthcare company built a federated multi-agent navigator on LangGraph + Deep Agents — and published the numbers
items.summary: A LangGraph "supergraph" routes to specialized sub-agents (urgent care, scheduling, specialist search, behavioral health) built by separate product teams, sharing tone and context through a filesystem-based skill registry; durable execution keeps full context across human handoffs. Four product teams migrated in 2 weeks with no regressions. Since launch: 75% lift in chat engagement, over 95% agreement with the agent's routing calls, over 99% detection of high-risk situations.
items.why: A real production system solving the "many teams, one coherent agent" problem with a filesystem-as-shared-context pattern, backed by real numbers rather than a feature announcement.
items.action: Read the "Skills Registry" section on progressive skill-file loading via a virtual filesystem — a concrete pattern for the same cross-service agent-context problem that keeps coming up in multi-agent design.

items.title: Loop engineering — an agentic-loop technique for Claude Code past basic prompt engineering
items.summary: Builds an agentic loop — the agent makes a change, a separate check scores it, the change is kept only if the score improves — with a concrete Claude Code setup: a project-context skill, a build skill, a write-checks skill that locks checks before the agent can see them, a fresh builder agent per feature, and an "auto loop" that rewrites its own working method from what failed last round.
items.why: A specific, reproducible harness pattern for getting Claude Code to run unsupervised for hours without just hoping it stays on track.
items.action: About 13 minutes — skip to the setup walkthrough and the auto-loop demonstration if short on time.

eval.reason: A concrete, reproducible harness pattern, not a generic prompting-tips video.

items.title: Just-in-time memory — curating agent memory at read time, not write time
items.summary: Walks through a research paper proposing deferred memory curation: instead of distilling a finished task into a fixed summary immediately — before you know what future tasks will need — raw trajectories are stored and curation is deferred to read time, when the current task is known. The approach gains several points over existing methods across three agent benchmarks; even an untrained curator beats the baselines.
items.why: Flips the usual "summarize and forget the details" approach to agent memory on its head — the detail you'd normally throw away at write time turns out to be exactly what the next task needed.
items.action: About 4 minutes — short enough for one traffic light.

eval.reason: A specific mechanism (deferred curation) with named benchmark gains, not a generic news recap.
